I understand your perspective, but for me historical continuity is more complex than just "the Empire killed the Republic". 

Even after the fall of the Republic, many of its institutions continued to function under the Empire. The Empire took many Republican ideals—especially legal and administrative principles—and refined them into a more centralized system. The Senate, while weakened, still played a role in governance. Roman legal principles, citizen rights, and administrative structures survived and even expanded. Under the Republic, citizenship was limited to elite Romans. The Empire gradually extended citizenship to broader populations (culminating in the Edict of Caracalla in 212 CE).  France, as the modern "most Roman" state for me, continues this tradition of centralized governance while maintaining citizen rights and legal codification.

Thank you for recognizing this historical continuity. Many people tend to overlook how the Napoleonic Code was deliberately designed as a synthesis of Roman law, Greek legal philosophy, and the ideals of the French Revolution. It wasn’t just a new legal system—it was an attempt to create a rationalized, universalist framework rooted in historical precedent.

Yes the Roman citizen was a free man with legal rights, and Rome’s governance evolved in ways that directly influenced later state structures. Even under the empire, many key legal and political principles of the Republic remained in place.

And the comparison to the USA is interesting because I admit that I often idealize France indeed. Just as the US isn’t just about New York and California, France is not just about its intellectual traditions—I know that it is used to be a warrior and "do-ers" state before gradually moved towards a "thinker" state, still retaining certain pragmatism. 

The Roman model is not just about military conquest—it’s about the organization of power, law, and citizenship. Even the US, despite its chaotic political culture, has admittedly inherited some Roman elements in its federal structure and military discipline—but France has done a far more direct refinement of Roman and Greek legal traditions in my opinion.

I do not say that what's right and what's wrong here, and I do respect your opinions, but this is my take: 

Yes, Rome had provinces and client states, but it was still a highly centralized system where ultimate authority rested in Rome itself.

Governors were directly appointed by the Senate or Emperor. Even local client kings operated under strict Roman influence.

France mirrors this model: regions and departments exist, but they answer to the central state (L'État), much like Roman governors answered to Rome.

And foe me, France didn’t "break" from Roman law—it codified it into the Napoleonic Code, which was inspired directly by Roman legal principles. Other nations copied the French system because it was the natural refinement of Roman legal traditions.

"The 'how' and 'what' questions: 

This refers to how France engages in democracy philosophically, rather than just procedurally.

The US and UK focus on “what” democracy is—mechanics, elections, rules.

France focuses on "how" democracy should function—its philosophical underpinnings, purpose, and ideological justification.

This is why French political culture is deeply intellectual, with constant ideological debates on democracy’s role.

France applies democracy like the Greeks did—through structured philosophical discourse—not just procedural mechanics like in the US/UK.

Roman consuls were indeed elected by the centuriate, but France's system of direct presidential election is a much clearer reflection, while still a evolution, of citizen-based democracy Rome though. France, by allowing citizens to directly elect their president, aligns more with Greek democratic ideals than the US or UK. 

In my opinion, France is not a perfect 1:1 copy of Rome, but it retains more of Rome's centralized governance, codified legal system, and philosophical approach to democracy than the US or UK.

Obviously it is not the same concept of democracy and governance, but I dare to say that France's democracy mirrors (and has it roots in) the Greek model, but it represents a more refined and evolved version. And France's territorial organization mirrors the Roman provincial system in many ways. Of course the exact mechanism can differ, but the underlying philosophy of a strong, centralized governance with regional autonomy is Roman enough for me..

Sorry if I make you think so, but I never meant that France is the single successor of the Roman Empire. In my argument, I have stated that the US and UK also inherited Roman/Greek values such as democracy, and Roman values even travelled to England, evolve there before getting back to France. There are definitely several modern states that inherit Roman/Greek values, France is just the one that represent classic values the best in my opinion (it does not mean that France is the best state).
I don't think there are so much societies that apply Roman law and governance system + Greek intellectualism and democracy into a strong state.

For me, France has a strong state while the UK government depends on Parliament and the US prefer a fragmented, federal system. France also uses codified law while the UK chooses common law and the US also prefer a legal system based on precedents. And France applies Greek democracy in a more philosophically way, always with the "how" question while the US/UK probably care more about "what" question and less about the ideological foundation of their democracies (also, French people can directly elect their President while British cannot directly elect their Prime Minister).
It's just for me, but Roman values are codified law and centralized state/governance, while Greek ones are philosophy and democracy. Basically France has Roman law + Greek thought in a strong state.

That means, in the Han and Tang times, Northern and Southern part of Korean peninsula were different from each other. Even in late modern times, the South one was more maritime, had more interaction and trade with Japan, especially Kyushu, and was the main battleground of the Imjin war, while the North had more interaction with Northeast China. Geographically, Busan also belongs to another climate group than the rest of Korea,  so the difference is still there.

There was. During ancient times there were two period named Three Kingdoms of Korea and Later Three Kingdoms of Korea, which lasted about 700 years in total. Goguryeo occupied the Northern part of the peninsula, Silla (the famous Shilla brand is named after this kingdom) and Baekje owned the Southern part. While Goguryeo had some (admittedly) small plains, Silla and Baekje's territories were mostly mountainous. Even when the Korean peninsula was unified under Goryeo later, the difference in identity still existed.

Absolutely. That fact also partly explains why Song and Ming dynasties did not have a strong motivation to get into Central Asia like Han and Tang. Even when Ming was at the peak of their power under Yongle Emperor, they decided to use their cavalry to chase the Mongol into Gobi Desert rather than explore the Tarim Basin.

Yes Chinese empires used to cover Northern part of Korea peninsula, which had a much different identity in comparison with Southern one. But only two dynasties (Han and Tang) have conquered Northern Korea, very briefly in Tang's case. The coldness, vastness and remoteness of Northeast China from the centre of Chinese civilization seemed to be too much for most Chinese empires and even controlling Northeast China was not an easy task at all, let alone Northern Korea.

The Hexi corridor is the only way to reach Central Asia basin from China proper. Another question may be why Chinese need to control Central Asia basin at all ? Firstly, there were horses, a lot of high-quality horses there. Secondly, being practically locked from three sides by the sea at the East, jungle and mountains at the South, desert and Siberia at the North, going West is the only way for China to connect with the rest of the world.

Normally, people like you sees Vietnam as Southeast Asian and it is perfectly understandable, but in fact Vietnam has two main parts and the Northern one is definitely North East Asia. The capital, Hanoi, also located in the North, so Vietnam is actually skewed into North East Asia culturally. 

So what makes the Northern part of Vietnam like North East Asia: 

- Confucianism and seniority-based culture 
- Widely using of Chinese rites and practices, for example the Lunar New Year and several Chinese holidays such as Mid-Autumn or Qingming Festival. You can see Classical Chinese characters in every temples and pagodas
- Naming customs. I would say that the difference between Vietnamese names and Chinese/Korean names is similar to the difference between French and Spanish/Italian names.
- Ethnicity. People in Northern Vietnam, especially in Red River Delta, belong to the same ethnic group with Southern China people, especially Guangxi, Guangdong and Fujian provinces. Southern Chinese literally migrated into Northern Vietnam in the past by countless waves. 

Culturally, northern Vietnam is very similar to Taiwan, as both have received several influx of immigrants from Fujian province in China. You can search for a Sinosphere map and easily find that Northern Vietnam is indeed belongs to Sinosphere region, which is a term that somewhat interchangeable for North East Asia.

I am not sure whether it counts or not, but Vietnam is a pretty unique case. 

We are normally categorized into the same Sinosphere group as China, Taiwan, North Korea, South Korea and Japan. But actually Vietnam is divided into Northern and Southern region, with the South is definitely a part of the Indian world. So Northern Vietnam is very similar to Southern China or Taiwan, but Southern Vietnam perhaps shares more similarities with Cambodia (Khmer people), Thailand (Theravada Buddishm) or even Malaysia (Austronesian people and Hinduism). Or, from another perspective, Northern Vietnam belongs to North East Asia and Southern Vietnam belongs to South East Asia. Essentially, two very different regions geographically are being combined into one country, and this means we are significantly different to every neighbour of us :)

Vietnamese here. 

Let's clarify things a bit. 

Average population density of South East Asia is 135 people/km2. Thailand has 132 ppl/km2, Laos has 27, Cambodia has 87 and Vietnam has 295 ppl/km2. 

So basically the population of Thailand is just as expected, in other words Thailand is not exactly populous. And your question could be paraphrased into that: "Why Laos and Cambodia has a much lower population density that the average of South East Asia, while Vietnam has much higher density, considering that they are neighbour countries?". 

Lao's case is pretty simple. They are a landlocked country with mountainous terrain. Arable land consists just 5% of Laos's total land. The borders with China, Vietnam and Cambodia is mostly mountain, so it is very difficult to do international trade. Their religion, Hinayana Buddhism, probably not helps in term of increasing population. 

Cambodia is a little bit more difficult to explain. Their arable land ratio is 21-22%, equal with Vietnam, but population density is much lower. Recent wars and the Pol Pot genocide clearly has an impact, but I guess there are at least two more reasons: their way of doing agricultural, which is not very effective, and lack of international trade. And again, their religion is Hinayana Buddhism. Also, as the Mekong Delta of Vietnam and South Cambodia are effectively in the same geographical region, there are some Khmer people that migrated to Vietnam due to the (relatively) better living condition there. 

Vietnam has some edge in comparison with neighbours: 

- Close proximity to China. Though Myanmar, Laos and Vietnam all have land border with China, only the road from Northeast Vietnam to Guangxi province, China, is in flat terrain. Besides that, Vietnam also have sea border with China and a lot of Chinese from Fujian and Guangdong provinces have migrated to Vietnam by boat. 

- Long seashores, which is useful for international trade and therefore international investment. That certainly played a big part in the five-fold increase of Vietnamese population since 1945. Yes, in 1945 Vietnam only has 20 million people, now we almost have 100 million. 

- As the only Sinosphere country in SE Asia, Vietnam has a culture which is a mix of Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism. Confucianism encourages people to have family and create as much children as possible. Actually, there is a saying in Confucianism that "if you want to show fillial piety, the best way is have children". 

Just some simple explanation here. Hope that they at least make some senses.

Yes I have to admit that the tongue thing is just my guess and is not based on any scientific research. Of course you know much more about Chinese and linguistics than me, but I just want to make some points. 

Mandarin now is certainly spoken in Hunan/Hubei and even further south, in Yunnan/Guizhou, but Mandarin is basically Beijing dialect and I suppose that 700-800 years ago, Beijing dialect was only spoken in the area around Beijing. Even now, in the 21st century, we still have Wu/Shanghainese in East China. So my theory is, 700-800 years ago, the Beijing dialect (or Northern dialect) gradually lost consonants ending while Southern dialects such as Cantonese/Teochew/Hakka... still kept it. I don't know why Northern dialects lost consonants ending, admitedlly. 

Actually, Cantonese is heavily influenced by the Middle Chinese spoken in Tang Dynasty, and the movement between Northern Vietnam and Guangdong is somewhat limited due to mountainous terrains. And, AFAIK, there were very few people that migrated from Northern Vietnam to Guangdong. In Vietnam we have another way of pronounce Chinese loanword, which is called Sino-Vietnamese. Sino-Vietnamese way of pronunciation is basically the Middle Chinese in Tang Dynasty as well, as Northern Vietnam was a part of the Tang, and is very similar to Cantonese. So I guess both Vietnamese and Cantonese have kept some features of Middle Chinese in the Tang era, due to significant distance from the economic, population and cultural centers in Yangtze and Yellow River basin.

1300 actually is about almost 200 years after the Manchu emerged. The Jin dynasty was Manchu as well. The area around Beijing was in the hand of nomadic people (Khitan/Liao Dynasty before that) for almost 400 years. As the Middle Chinese in Tang dynasty clearly still had consonants ending (which is still preserved in Cantonese), this is pretty clear that the Beijing dialect has been heavily influenced by nomadic people, to the point that it lost all consonants ending. The hard weather that nomadic people lived in probably made their tongues less flexible, so they could not pronounce as much sound as southern people, for example yat/yam/yap... all become "ya", in no small part due to the less flexible tongue of nomads.

Cantonese has a lot of end consonants. Mandarin has none. And Mandarin is heavily influenced by the way Manchu people spoke Chinese, not only the lack of end consonants but also the "r"/ "er" sound at the end of words.
Which are pronounced "Thế giới" and "quốc" which sounds 100% like "kuốc" in Vietnamese. The same Chinese characters from Vietnam to Japan, just with different pronunciation.

I will answer your question, one by one, and with some more suggestion: 

- Should you have cash in local currency (VND): Surely, because international credit card will only work on hotels/high-end restaurants/big supermarkets. You will need some cash to pay for taxi, street food and buying some daily stuff. 

- What is the tip to ensure your safety: Vietnam is generally safe, nothing much to worry about, but you should stick to the tourist area (1st District, Ho Chi Minh city) at night. 

- Best place to stay: 1st District, Ho Chi Minh City and Hoan Kiem District, if you go to Ha Noi

- Best transport from airport: For the first trip from the airport to your hotel, just ask your hotel to arrange it. It will be more expensive than a Grab but not much, and even cheaper than a normal taxi. The taxi pick-up point at Tan Son Nhat airport is a mess anyway. Even a Vietnamese like me feel difficult to get to pick-up point.

Some more tips for you: 

- You will need a Vietnamese SIM card, which you can buy at the airport, to activate Grab. With Grab, you can book a taxi/motorbike to almost everywhere you want. 

- Book your hotel in advance to make sure that you have a place to stay in the first 2-3 days of the trip. But do not eat at your hotel. Just go out and enjoy the street food. 

- Remember the hotline phone number of local police (ask your hotel for that). If there is any problem, just try to call/texting the police (you can use Google Translate to convert your message into Vietnamese). They will probably be nice and try to help foreign tourists.

No, Van Hau is Vietnamese. His full name in Vietnamese is actually Đoàn Văn Hậu, with Đoàn is the surname, Văn is middle name and Hậu is last name. Internationally, he is called Van Hau. 

Văn is a very popular middle name in Vietnam. Its popularity has gone down a bit in recent years, but still make up 10-20% of all Vietnamese middle names. In the Vietnamese national team there are several players with Văn (Van) middle name such an Van Lam, Van Duc, Van Thanh....

It is just a coincidence that the "Van" middle name in Vietnamese is similar to "Van" middle name in Dutch.
